claims.text: Standard casting or homogenization produces a mostly single-phase or coarsely phase-separated high-entropy-alloy microstructure.
The proposed multi-step thermal protocol will induce a controlled dual-phase microstructure.
The proposed aging treatment will induce nanoscale precipitation.
Subcritical annealing will optimize the precipitate distribution.
Tight regulation of temperature and time is required to obtain an optimal precipitate volume fraction and size.
Over-aging or insufficient nucleation can create microstructural inhomogeneity.
Microstructural inhomogeneity caused by processing deviations can negate the mechanical-property improvements or reduce ductility.
Uniformly dispersed nanoscale precipitates impede dislocation motion.
Uniformly dispersed nanoscale precipitates impede or deflect crack propagation.
Dislocation pinning by nanoscale precipitates raises yield strength.
Crack deflection by nanoscale precipitates raises fracture toughness.
A sufficiently ductile matrix allows strengthening by precipitates without sacrificing ductility.
The dual-phase precipitate-containing framework preserves or slightly enhances Young's modulus.
The processed alloy will have higher yield strength than the conventionally processed single-phase control.
The processed alloy will have greater tensile ductility than the conventionally processed single-phase control.
The processed alloy will have improved or maintained Young's modulus relative to the conventionally processed single-phase control.
The processed alloy will have greater fracture resistance than the conventionally processed single-phase control.
The improvements may extend from room temperature to lower temperatures.
The proposed effects may fail when alloy composition is outside the range that permits nanoscale precipitate formation.
Aggressive aging can coarsen precipitates and thereby reduce ductility and toughness.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis predicts an improvement in Young's modulus, whereas the predicted outcome allows Young's modulus merely to be maintained.

The hypothesis claims simultaneous improvement in all four target properties, but the falsification rule only requires statistically significant improvement in at least two properties to avoid falsification.
